input.area_summary: The quality-management lineage fills the governance gap in the existing report: it is the one surveyed tradition whose core artifact is the controlled definition itself. Three contributions stand out. (1) ISO 9001:2015 clause 7.5 plus the ISO 9000:2015 vocabulary supply the established form for governing versioned definition surfaces — the controlled-document regime (identification, format, review-and-approval, version control, availability-at-point-of-use, obsolete-document prevention, external-origin control) and the load-bearing maintain-vs-retain distinction between living definitions and immutable records. (2) The Shewhart(1939)→Deming-wheel(1950)→PDCA(1951/Ishikawa 1985)→PDSA(1986–1993)/Model-for-Improvement lineage supplies the improvement-loop FORM, with two structural facts the shop needs: Shewhart's circle is the original statement that specification precedes production precedes inspection and that inspection feeds re-specification; and the loop's terminal phase (PDCA Act, DMAIC Control) is defined as a document-control action — standardize the change into the governed surface — so improvement loops close in ratified-definition revisions, not ad-hoc fixes. PDSA's prediction-then-Study discipline is the established form for the judge-calibration loop the report already requires (EvalGen). (3) Six Sigma's CTQ tree is the strongest external analogue to derive-checks-from-ratified-definitions found in any tradition surveyed: a traceability tree from qualitative customer need through quality drivers to measurable requirements with pass criteria, converging exactly with Deming's operational definition already adopted in report §2.5(a); DMAIC contributes the phase-gate form where gates check deliverables (not activity) and are reviewed by an authority seat distinct from the performer. All phase names, page numbers, and clause facts below were verified against the cited sources this session (the Moen PDSA history paper was retrieved in full; paywalled ISO clause detail was cross-verified via the official ISO/TC 176 public guidance and multiple consistent secondary sources, noted per finding).

findings.name: ISO 9001:2015 clause 7.5 — documented information (controlled-document regime)
findings.citation: ISO 9001:2015, Quality management systems — Requirements, clause 7.5 (iso.org/standard/62085.html). Official public companion: ISO/TC 176/SC2/N1286, Guidance on the requirements for Documented Information of ISO 9001:2015 (iso.org/iso/documented_information.pdf). Clause detail cross-verified via N1286 and consistent secondary sources; the standard text itself is paywalled.
findings.what_it_defines: The requirements regime for controlled documents. 7.5.1: the QMS includes documented information required by the standard PLUS whatever the organization determines necessary for effectiveness (extent proportional to organization size, process complexity, competence). 7.5.2 (creating and updating): ensure (a) identification and description (e.g. title, date, author, reference number), (b) format (e.g. language, software version, graphics) and media (paper, electronic), (c) review and approval for suitability and adequacy. 7.5.3 (control): information must be available and suitable for use where and when needed, and adequately protected (loss of confidentiality, improper use, loss of integrity); control activities as applicable: distribution/access/retrieval/use; storage and preservation including legibility; control of changes (e.g. version control); retention and disposition. Documented information of external origin determined necessary must be identified and controlled; information retained as evidence of conformity must be protected from unintended alteration. The 2015 edition merged 'documents' and 'records' into one concept, 'documented information', with two verbs carrying the old distinction: MAINTAIN (keep current — definitional documents) vs RETAIN (keep as evidence — records).
form_elements: Two-tier scope rule: standard-required information + organization-determined-necessary information, extent proportional to complexity
Creation/update triple: identification-and-description, format-and-media, review-and-approval for suitability and adequacy
Availability rule: relevant version available at point of use, when needed
Obsolete-document rule: prevent unintended use of superseded versions
Change control: changes identified, current revision status known (version control named explicitly)
Control-activity checklist: distribution, access (view-only vs view-and-change), retrieval and use, storage and preservation, retention and disposition
External-origin documents identified and brought under control
Evidence records protected from unintended alteration
maintain (keep current) vs retain (keep as evidence) verb distinction
findings.fit_notes: Direct model for governing versioned prompt/skill/definition surfaces. The mapping is one-to-one: the definition corpus is 'documented information determined necessary'; ratification = review-and-approval for suitability and adequacy; the compiled-context assembly guarantee = relevant-version-available-at-point-of-use; the stale-compiled-prompt hazard = the obsolete-document rule; git + pinning (report §2.7, Langfuse algebra) = change control and revision status; canonical templates from shopsystem-templates = external-origin control; protection-from-unintended-alteration = the immutability rule for ADRs/session records. What ISO adds over what the report already has is the requirements CHECKLIST form — clause 7.5 is itself a derivable audit rubric for the governance layer, and audit traceability (which version was in force when a given artifact was produced) is exactly the judge-model/prompt-version pinning requirement of §2.6/§3. ADAPT: take the requirement checklist and the maintain/retain distinction; drop certification machinery, and let git supply the mechanics ISO leaves to procedure.

findings.name: ISO 9000:2015 vocabulary (documented information, record, verification/validation term system)
findings.citation: ISO 9000:2015, Quality management systems — Fundamentals and vocabulary, 4th ed., September 2015, clause 3 (iso.org/standard/45481.html; full text publicly readable on the ISO Online Browsing Platform). Term numbers 3.8.5/3.8.6/3.8.10 verified this session; other terms cited by name.
findings.what_it_defines: The controlled term system beneath document control and checking: document = 'information and the medium on which it is contained' (3.8.5); documented information = 'information required to be controlled and maintained by an organization and the medium on which it is contained' (3.8.6); record = 'document stating results achieved or providing evidence of activities performed' (3.8.10); specification = a document stating requirements; plus the linked cluster: requirement (need or expectation that is stated, generally implied or obligatory), conformity/nonconformity (fulfilment / non-fulfilment of a requirement), objective evidence, verification (confirmation via objective evidence that SPECIFIED REQUIREMENTS are fulfilled) vs validation (confirmation via objective evidence that requirements for a SPECIFIC INTENDED USE are fulfilled). Definitions are themselves written in a controlled defined-term-references-defined-term style.
form_elements: document / documented information / record as distinct defined terms
record defined by function: states results achieved or evidences activities performed
specification = document stating requirements
conformity = fulfilment of a requirement (the semantic of every check verdict)
verification vs validation split: against stated requirements vs against intended use
objective evidence as the admissibility condition for both
vocabulary itself maintained as a controlled, cross-referenced term system
findings.fit_notes: ADOPT as citable vocabulary anchors. Three distinctions do real work for the shop: (1) maintained-definition vs retained-record formalizes the split the report already draws in §2.4 (principles amended under change control vs ADRs immutable and superseded) and generalizes it to every artifact kind; (2) verification vs validation maps precisely onto mechanical-checks-against-the-definition vs fitness-judgment-against-intended-use (the §2.6 judged fitness tests are validation, the derived lint/schema checks are verification — naming this prevents category errors in check design); (3) conformity-as-fulfilment-of-a-requirement plus the objective-evidence condition restates the report's Deming operational-definition rule (§2.5a) in standards language. Costs nothing to adopt; the terms are stable, public, and already implicit in the system.

findings.name: ISO 10013:2021 — Guidance for documented information
findings.citation: ISO 10013:2021, Quality management systems — Guidance for documented information, 1st ed., March 2021, 14 pp. (iso.org/standard/75736.html; replaces ISO/TR 10013:2001). Existence, edition, committee, and scope verified; full text paywalled.
findings.what_it_defines: The how-to companion to 9001 clause 7.5: guidance on developing and maintaining the documented information a QMS needs, tailored to the organization — the traditional documentation hierarchy (policy / manual at the top, procedures, work instructions, forms and records at the bottom: altitude decreasing, specificity increasing), plus creation, revision-control, and distribution practice, updated in 2021 for digitized documentation and automated process-flow control.
form_elements: Documentation hierarchy: policy → procedure → work instruction → form/record (decreasing altitude, increasing specificity)
Guidance-not-requirements posture: one authoritative requirements clause (9001 7.5) with a separate non-binding practice guide
Tailoring rule: documentation extent fits the organization, not a fixed template
findings.fit_notes: CONTEXT-ONLY. The hierarchy idea (principle → process definition → skill body → record) parallels structures the report already anchors better elsewhere (15289 for artifact schemas, Agent Skills for the operational layer), and the 14-page guidance adds little beyond clause 7.5 itself. Its one citable structural lesson is the normative/informative split at the standards-architecture level: requirements live in one controlled place (9001 7.5) and practice guidance is a separate, subordinate, non-binding document — the same WCAG-style split the report adopts in §2.5(f). Cite it to show the document-control tradition itself observes construction-definition-precedes-guidance; do not adopt its content.

findings.name: Shewhart cycle (specification–production–inspection, 1939)
findings.tradition: Statistical quality control (Bell Labs / USDA Graduate School)
findings.citation: Shewhart, W. A., Statistical Method from the Viewpoint of Quality Control, The Graduate School, U.S. Department of Agriculture, 1939 (Dover reprint 1986), p. 45; edited by W. Edwards Deming. Quotation and page verified via Moen, 'Foundation and History of the PDSA Cycle', Associates in Process Improvement (deming.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/PDSA_History_Ron_Moen.pdf), retrieved in full this session.
findings.what_it_defines: The original improvement-loop form. Shewhart takes the three mass-production steps — specification, production, inspection — and rules: 'These three steps must go in a circle instead of in a straight line... specification, production, and inspection correspond respectively to making a hypothesis, carrying out an experiment, and testing the hypothesis. The three steps constitute a dynamic scientific process of acquiring knowledge.' Each phase is epistemically typed (hypothesis / experiment / test), and inspection's output is not a verdict alone but input to re-specification.
form_elements: Three phases: specification (hypothesis), production (experiment), inspection (test)
Ordering rule: specification precedes production precedes inspection
Circularity rule: inspection feeds re-specification; the line becomes a loop
Epistemic typing: each phase identified with a scientific-method step, making the loop a knowledge-acquisition process
findings.fit_notes: This is the primary-source ancestor of the shop's re-founding commitment: construction-definitions-precede-checks IS Shewhart's ordering (specification precedes inspection; inspection is meaningful only against a specification), and his circularity rule adds the closure the report currently leaves implicit — check results must be able to revise the ratified definition, under change control, or the loop is broken. ADAPT as a citable foundational principle plus one structural requirement: every derived check traces back to a specification clause, and every check outcome has a defined path back into specification revision. Not a process container (that role stays with 24774/ETVX per §2.1); it is the warrant beneath them.

findings.name: Deming wheel (1950) → Japanese PDCA (1951; Ishikawa 1985) — Act-as-standardization improvement loop
findings.citation: Deming, W. E., Elementary Principles of the Statistical Control of Quality, JUSE, 1950 (the eight-day JUSE seminar wheel: design with tests → make/test → sell → test in service through market research → redesign); Imai, M., Kaizen: The Key to Japan's Competitive Success, Random House, 1986, p. 60 (Japanese executives' recasting of the wheel as Plan–Do–Check–Act); Ishikawa, K., What Is Total Quality Control? The Japanese Way, Prentice-Hall, 1985, pp. 56–61 (PDCA subdivided: goals+methods, training+implementation, check effects, act). All as documented in Moen, 'Foundation and History of the PDSA Cycle' (deming.org), retrieved in full this session.
findings.what_it_defines: The PDCA form and, critically, where each phase's outputs live. Plan: definition of the problem, goals and targets, and the METHODS for reaching them (Ishikawa; traceable to Mizuno 1959) — the plan phase's output is itself a standard-to-be. Do: education/training plus implementation. Check: evaluation of results against the plan. Act: 'back to plan if the results are unsatisfactory, or STANDARDIZATION if the results are satisfactory' — PDCA 'emphasized the prevention of error recurrence by establishing standards and the ongoing modification of those standards' (Moen), with Ishikawa adding that good control means standards revised constantly to reflect consumer voices and next-process requirements. In Japanese practice each loop turn is documented in the QC-story format alongside the seven basic tools (Lillrank & Kano 1989, per Moen).
form_elements: Four phases: Plan (problem, goals, methods) / Do (train, implement) / Check (evaluate) / Act (standardize or re-plan)
Terminal-phase rule: a successful loop turn ENDS in a document-control action — the change is written into the standard
Failure path defined: unsatisfactory results loop back to Plan, not to ad-hoc patching
Standards are living: revised continuously from downstream voices (consumer complaints, next process)
QC story as the per-turn documented record of the loop
findings.fit_notes: ADAPT as the shape of the shop's improvement loop over its definition surfaces. The load-bearing element is Act-as-standardization: a finding from any check or reconciliation is not closed until the governed surface (definition, skill, prompt, fitness set) is revised and re-ratified — or the finding is explicitly sent back to Plan. This gives the report's Fagan-style checklist-item add/retire rule (§2.5d) and criteria-drift calibration loop (§3) their missing outer loop and names its termination condition. The QC-story precedent maps to the existing session-record/finding artifact kinds: one documented record per loop turn. Drop the statistical seven-tools apparatus; keep the loop skeleton, the two exit paths, and the standards-are-living rule (which matches TOGAF's Stable-but-amendable, already adopted in §2.4).

findings.name: Deming PDSA (1986/1993) and the Model for Improvement (prediction-driven learning loop)
findings.tradition: Deming; Associates in Process Improvement / IHI improvement science
findings.citation: Deming, W. E., Out of the Crisis, MIT Press, 1986, p. 88 (Shewhart cycle reintroduced); Deming, W. E., The New Economics, MIT Press, 1993, p. 135 ('Shewhart Cycle for Learning and Improvement — the PDSA Cycle'; Deming to Moen, 17 Nov 1990: 'be sure to call it PDSA, not the corruption PDCA'); Moen, Nolan, Provost, Improving Quality Through Planned Experimentation, McGraw-Hill, 1991, p. 11 (prediction added to Plan); Langley, Nolan, Nolan, 'The Foundation of Improvement', Quality Progress, June 1994, p. 81; Langley et al., The Improvement Guide, 2nd ed., Jossey-Bass, 2009, p. 24 (Model for Improvement). All verified via Moen's PDSA history paper (deming.org), retrieved in full this session.
findings.what_it_defines: The learning variant of the loop, distinct from PDCA by Deming's own insistence (he called PDCA unrelated to his cycle: 'They bear no relation to each other', GAO roundtable 1980). Plan: plan a change or test aimed at improvement, INCLUDING a stated prediction and the theory behind it (Moen/Nolan/Provost 1991). Do: carry it out, preferably small scale. Study (not Check — 'check' means 'to hold back'): compare observed results against the prediction — the deductive/inductive interplay that produces learning. Act: adopt, abandon, or run the cycle again under different conditions. The Model for Improvement (1994) frames every cycle with three questions: What are we trying to accomplish? How will we know that a change is an improvement? What change can we make that will result in improvement? Moen's summary of the division of labor: PDCA is used for implementation and compliance; PDSA for testing and implementing (learning).
form_elements: Plan requires a written prediction plus its theory, before execution
Do is deliberately small-scale (pilot before adoption)
Study compares observed against predicted — not merely 'did it work'
Act has three defined outcomes: adopt / abandon / re-run under changed conditions
Three framing questions, the second being an explicit check-derivation question ('How will we know that a change is an improvement?')
Two distinct loops for two jobs: PDSA for testing/learning, PDCA for standardization/compliance
findings.fit_notes: ADAPT, with a precise assignment: the shop needs BOTH loops, and this lineage names the difference. PDCA (previous finding) governs standardization of ratified definitions; PDSA is the established form for the judge-calibration and criteria-drift loop the report already requires (§2.6, §3: EvalGen's iterative human-calibration loop IS a PDSA cycle once named). Concretely: a fitness-set or judge-prompt revision should record a prediction (which verdicts will change and why) before deployment, and its Study step compares sampled product-authority grading against that prediction — turning open question 7 (calibration governance) from an ownership question into a form with defined phase outputs. Question 2 of the Model for Improvement is a one-line warrant for the whole re-founding: no change without a stated way of knowing, i.e. no definition without derivable checks.

findings.name: CTQ (critical-to-quality) tree — need → driver → measurable requirement derivation
findings.tradition: Six Sigma (Motorola/GE lineage); ancestor in QFD
findings.citation: ASQ Quality Glossary, 'critical to quality' (asq.org/quality-resources/quality-glossary): CTQs are the 'key measurable characteristics of a product or process whose performance standards or specification limits must be met in order to satisfy the customer'. Authoritative handbook treatment: Kubiak & Benbow, The Certified Six Sigma Black Belt Handbook, 3rd ed., ASQ Quality Press, 2016 (ISBN 9780873899413, aligned to the ASQ CSSBB Body of Knowledge); Pande, Neuman, Cavanagh, The Six Sigma Way: How GE, Motorola, and Other Top Companies Are Honing Their Performance, McGraw-Hill, 2000 (VOC-to-CTQ translation in GE-lineage practice). Matrix ancestor: Hauser & Clausing, 'The House of Quality', Harvard Business Review 66(3), May–June 1988, pp. 63–73 (hbr.org/1988/05/the-house-of-quality). No single primary inventor source exists for the tree itself — it is GE-era practice; ASQ is the authoritative secondary anchor.
findings.what_it_defines: The canonical derivation from qualitative to checkable, as a three-level tree with traceability: (1) NEED — the customer's requirement in the customer's qualitative language; (2) DRIVERS — the quality characteristics by which the customer will judge whether the need is met; (3) CTQ PERFORMANCE REQUIREMENTS — for each driver, one or more measurable characteristics, each with a specification limit or target that operationalizes 'good enough'. The admissibility rule is that leaves must be measurable; the structural rule is that every leaf traces up through a driver to a stated need, and drilling stops when a requirement is concrete enough to measure against. QFD's House of Quality is the denser matrix ancestor: weighted customer attributes crossed with engineering characteristics carrying objective target values.
form_elements: Three fixed levels: qualitative need → quality drivers → measurable requirements
Leaf admissibility rule: a leaf is a measurable characteristic with a specification limit/target, or the derivation is unfinished
Full traceability: every check traces to a driver, every driver to a need
Coverage test in both directions: a need with no leaves is unmeasured; a leaf with no need is unauthorized
Derivation performed in the Define phase, i.e. before measurement or improvement work begins
findings.fit_notes: The strongest single-form analogue found in any tradition to the shop's derive-checks-from-ratified-definitions move. Mapping: ratified construction definition = need level; the definition's stated qualities/outcomes = drivers; each derived mechanical check or rubric item = a CTQ leaf, admissible only once operationalized — which is exactly Deming's operational definition already adopted in §2.5(a), and the concrete table form that open question 6 (outcome→indicator→rubric traceability ceremony) asks for. ADAPT: adopt the three-level derivation record and both coverage tests per artifact kind (a small need→driver→check table stored with the fitness set, giving 330xx-style traceability without assessor machinery); drop sigma-level targets and statistical capability apparatus, and treat rubric anchors (Ragas/Brookhart forms, §2.5b) as the specification-limit analogue for qualitative leaves.

findings.name: DMAIC — defined process with phase deliverables and tollgate reviews
findings.citation: ASQ, 'DMAIC Process: Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control' (asq.org/quality-resources/dmaic); Kubiak & Benbow, The Certified Six Sigma Black Belt Handbook, 3rd ed., ASQ Quality Press, 2016 (organized to the ASQ CSSBB Body of Knowledge, which is itself structured by DMAIC phase); Pande, Neuman, Cavanagh, The Six Sigma Way, McGraw-Hill, 2000. Tollgate vocabulary confirmed in ASQ practice materials (ASQ section greenbelt 'Define Tollgate' curriculum).
findings.what_it_defines: A data-driven improvement process for existing processes, defined as five phases each specified by its deliverables rather than its activities: Define (project charter, voice of customer and CTQs, high-level process map); Measure (baseline performance, operational definitions of the measures, measurement-system validation); Analyze (root causes identified and verified with data); Improve (solutions implemented and validated against the baseline); Control (control plan, standardized and documented process, monitoring installed, handoff to the process owner). Phase boundaries carry tollgate reviews: a formal checkpoint where an authority seat distinct from the team doing the work (sponsor/champion/Master Black Belt) reviews the phase deliverables for completeness and quality and formally authorizes entry to the next phase.
form_elements: Five named phases, each defined by exit deliverables, not activity lists
Tollgate/phase-gate: deliverable review at each boundary, pass required to proceed
Separation of seats: gate review is performed by an authority distinct from the performer
Measure phase institutionalizes operational definitions and measurement-system validation before any judgment of the process
Control phase termination rule: the effort is not complete until the change is standardized into controlled documentation with monitoring in place and ownership transferred
findings.fit_notes: ADAPT selectively; as a process container it mostly reinforces forms the report already chose (deliverable-defined phases ≈ 24774 outcomes plus ETVX exit criteria, §2.1). Three elements are independently adoptable: (1) the distinct-seat tollgate — gate review by an authority other than the producer — maps directly onto product-authority ratification of definitions and the lead/BC review split, and is the established name for that governance shape; (2) Measure-before-Analyze, with measurement-system validation, is the process-level form of judge calibration: validate the judge/check before trusting its verdicts about artifacts; (3) the Control-phase termination rule independently converges with PDCA's Act-as-standardization — in this whole lineage, improvement work terminates in a document-control action on a governed surface, which is precisely the closure rule the shop's quality layer should ratify. Do not adopt belt hierarchy, project-charter ceremony, or the statistical toolkit.
